extracted.intended_audience: evolutionary biologists, naturalists, and students of organic evolution
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how to study and explain the causes of organic evolution: prefer concrete, measurable physical agencies and account for both differential (selective) and universal (medium-driven) effects. Uses physical analogies and empirical examples to illustrate methodological principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve vague causes into definite physical factors
rubrics_metrics.description: When we insist on resolving a verbally-intelligible cause into its actual factors, we get not only a clear solution of the problem before us, but we find that the way is opened to solutions of sundry other problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the plumber's vague 'suction' explanation versus the physicist's account (atmospheric pressure, columns of air, barometer, pump limit ~32 feet). Anti-pattern: accepting familiar-sounding labels (e.g. 'suction') without analyzing the measurable forces at work. Benefit: yields clearer understanding and connects to other phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame growth, variation, survival, death as effects of definite agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Growth, variation, survival, death, if they are to be reduced to the forms in which physical science can recognize them, must be expressed as effects of agencies definitely conceived — mechanical forces, light, heat, chemical affinity, &c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat biological phenomena as joint operations of forces on materials. Methodological implication: identify the relevant physical/chemical forces and materials when explaining changes in structure or life-history traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid personification and anthropocentric metaphors (e.g., 'Nature selects')
rubrics_metrics.description: The words 'natural selection' do not express a cause in the physical sense. The tacitly implied Nature which selects is not an embodied agency analogous to the man who selects artificially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: speaking as if Nature or 'survival' are intentional agents. Instead, represent selection as the effect of concrete co-operating actions (overthrowing individuals by environmental agencies). Use precise mechanistic language rather than personifying metaphors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious with 'survival of the fittest'—recognize figurative meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'fittest' as thus used is a figure of speech; suggesting that amid surrounding actions, an organism characterized by the word has either a greater ability than others ... to maintain the equilibrium of its vital activities, or else has so much greater a power of multiplication ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume a single physical concept of 'fitness'; it can cover different cases (longevity vs fertility). Explicitly state which property (e.g., maintenance of internal equilibrium, reproductive rate) is meant in an analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for both differential (selective) and uniform (medium-driven) effects
rubrics_metrics.description: While selective actions of the environment separate organisms (differential effects), the simultaneous indiscriminate actions produce a unity of character (universal likeness) among them; the general and constant operation of environmental agencies produces primary and universal effects often overlooked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: when explaining evolutionary change, identify which effects arise from differential resistance (leading to selection) and which arise from uniform, pervasive action of the medium (leading to common primary traits). Example: sea sorting pebbles (differential sorting) vs. rounding and smoothing (uniform action).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish direct action of conditions from natural selection
rubrics_metrics.description: The direct action of the conditions of life, whether leading to definite or indefinite results, is a totally distinct consideration from the effects of natural selection; changed conditions of life have acted so definitely and powerfully on the organisation of our domesticated productions that they have sufficed to form new sub-varieties or races, without the aid of selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat changes due to climate, food, or other environmental conditions as mechanisms in their own right. Use empirical examples (maize transformed in a few generations; American vs European trees grown side-by-side) to substantiate direct environmental effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt an exclusively physical point of view for studying organism–medium interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: I have elaborated this criticism with the intention of emphasizing the need for studying the changes which have gone on, and are ever going on, in organic bodies, from an exclusively physical point of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze organismal change by considering concrete physical forces and chemical interactions rather than relying on biological metaphors. This reveals additional effects not captured by selection-focused narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider surface-vs-interior differential action of the medium
rubrics_metrics.description: The most general trait is the greater amount of change wrought on the outer surface than on the inner mass; the primary and almost universal effect of the converse between the body and its medium is to differentiate its outside from its inside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate how exposure leads to outer-part differentiation (cell walls, envelopes, surface rust, weathering) and how this fundamental pattern shapes primary traits in organisms (cellular envelopes in protophytes, encystment in protozoa). Use inorganic analogies (rusted cannon-ball, exfoliation of granite) and cellular observations to support inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study combined effects of multiple environmental forces and matters
rubrics_metrics.description: When the respective effects of gravitation, heat, light, &c., are studied, as well as the respective effects, physical and chemical, of the matters forming the media, water and air, it will be found that while more or less operative on all bodies, each modifies organic bodies to an extent immensely greater than the extent to which it modifies inorganic bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: assess the joint and individual roles of forces (gravity, heat, light) and media (water, air, chemical composition) in producing changes. Recognize organic materials' greater modifiability and that interactions among these factors can produce complex outcomes.
